title: Marine Radar and ARPA
description: Test your understanding of marine radar, radar controls, display modes, target tracking, CPA, TCPA, ARPA limitations and practical collision-risk assessment.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of marine radar?
options: To measure the vessel's fuel consumption
To detect and display targets using reflected radio energy
To transmit the vessel's identity to nearby ships
To calculate cargo stability
questions.explanation: Marine radar transmits radio pulses and displays echoes reflected from ships, land and other objects.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of ARPA?
options: To automatically track radar targets and calculate their movement
To replace the vessel's steering system
To transmit navigational warnings
To control the radar antenna speed
questions.explanation: ARPA tracks selected targets and calculates information such as course, speed, CPA and TCPA.

questions.question: What does CPA mean?
options: Course Prediction Alarm
Closest Point of Approach
Calculated Position Accuracy
Coastal Passage Area
questions.explanation: CPA is the predicted minimum distance between own ship and a tracked target if both maintain their current movement.

questions.question: What does TCPA indicate?
options: The target's true course
The time remaining until the predicted closest point of approach
The distance to the target at present
The time since the target was first detected
questions.explanation: TCPA is the predicted time until CPA occurs.

questions.question: Which radar band generally provides better target definition in normal conditions?
options: S-band
X-band
MF-band
VHF-band
questions.explanation: X-band radar normally provides finer target definition because of its shorter wavelength.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the radar gain control?
options: To adjust receiver sensitivity and the strength of displayed echoes
To change the vessel's heading input
To control antenna rotation speed
To set the target's predicted course
questions.explanation: Gain controls receiver sensitivity. Too little gain may hide weak targets, while excessive gain may create background noise.

questions.question: Which control is primarily used to reduce echoes caused by waves close to the vessel?
options: Rain clutter control
Sea clutter control
Pulse length selector
Heading marker control
questions.explanation: Sea clutter control reduces unwanted echoes caused by waves, particularly near own ship.

questions.question: What is a major advantage of S-band radar in heavy rain?
options: It normally suffers less attenuation and rain clutter than X-band radar
It always detects smaller targets more clearly
It does not require gain adjustment
It automatically calculates CPA without ARPA
questions.explanation: The longer wavelength of S-band radar generally provides better performance through heavy rain and precipitation.

questions.question: What does a relative-motion radar display show?
options: Own ship moving across a stationary chart
Own ship fixed while other targets move relative to it
Only the true courses of tracked vessels
The movement of land relative to north
questions.explanation: In relative motion, own ship remains fixed on the display while targets move according to their relative movement.

questions.question: Why should radar plotting or systematic target observation be used?
options: To determine whether a target presents a risk of collision
To identify the target's cargo
To calculate the target's draft
To determine the target's flag State
questions.explanation: Repeated observations or plotting are needed to assess target movement, bearing trend, CPA and collision risk.

questions.question: A target remains on a nearly constant bearing while its range steadily decreases. What does this most strongly indicate?
options: The target is moving away from own ship
A possible risk of collision exists
The radar heading input has failed
The target is stationary
questions.explanation: A constant or nearly constant bearing with decreasing range is a classic indication of collision risk.

questions.question: An ARPA target displays CPA 0.2 NM and TCPA 10 minutes. What is the correct interpretation?
options: The target is currently 0.2 NM away
The target is predicted to pass 0.2 NM away in approximately 10 minutes
The target will alter course in 10 minutes
Own ship must alter course by 0.2 degrees
questions.explanation: CPA is the predicted passing distance, while TCPA is the predicted time until that closest approach.

questions.question: After own ship makes a large alteration of course, why may ARPA target data be temporarily unreliable?
options: ARPA requires time to recalculate target movement using the new own-ship data
Radar cannot transmit while the rudder is moving
All targets automatically change their true course
The radar antenna stops during alterations
questions.explanation: Following manoeuvres, ARPA needs time and valid sensor data to stabilize and recalculate vectors, CPA and TCPA.

questions.question: Heavy rain causes large areas of clutter on the radar display. What is the best initial response?
options: Increase gain to maximum
Adjust rain clutter carefully while ensuring genuine targets remain visible
Switch off the radar until the rain passes
Reduce the range scale to zero
questions.explanation: Rain clutter control should be adjusted carefully because excessive suppression may also remove genuine targets.

questions.question: A small target close to a large vessel disappears temporarily from the display. Which radar limitation is the most plausible explanation?
options: Target masking or shadowing by the larger vessel
Second-trace echo
Multiple echo
Incorrect pulse length
questions.explanation: A larger target may mask a smaller nearby target or create an area where the smaller echo cannot be distinguished.

questions.question: Several equally spaced echoes appear beyond a large nearby target on the same bearing. What are they most likely to be?
options: Side-lobe echoes
Multiple echoes
AIS targets
Second-trace echoes
questions.explanation: Multiple echoes can occur when radar energy reflects repeatedly between own ship and a large nearby target.

questions.question: A strong false echo appears at the same range as a real target but on a slightly different bearing. Which phenomenon may cause this?
options: Side-lobe echoes
Sea stabilization
True-motion reset
Target swap
questions.explanation: Side lobes can produce false echoes around strong targets, often at the same range but on different bearings.

questions.question: An ARPA-tracked target passes very close to another target and the displayed vectors appear to exchange between them. What has most likely occurred?
options: Second-trace interference
Target swap
Sea clutter
Radar shadowing
questions.explanation: Target swap occurs when the tracking system confuses two close targets and transfers tracking data from one echo to another.

questions.question: Why should ARPA information not be used as the sole basis for collision-avoidance decisions?
options: ARPA data depends on correct sensor inputs, target tracking and operator settings
ARPA only functions in port
ARPA cannot calculate target speed
ARPA information is not permitted under COLREG
questions.explanation: ARPA is an aid. Errors in heading, speed, tracking, stabilization or operator settings can produce misleading information, so all available means must be used.

questions.question: In restricted visibility, a radar target is detected forward of the beam and collision risk is developing. Which principle is most appropriate?
options: Maintain course and speed because the target is not visually observed
Assess the situation using radar and take appropriate avoiding action in accordance with the COLREGs
Alter course to port in every situation
Rely only on the target's AIS information
questions.explanation: A vessel detecting another vessel by radar in restricted visibility must determine whether collision risk exists and take appropriate action under Rule 19.
